chmmc-2019-power-01.title: Strips cut by diagonals
chmmc-2019-power-01.body: Write $n=2k$. Cut the unit square into $k$ vertical rectangles of width $\frac1k$ and height $1$, each of area $\frac1k$. Cut each rectangle along a diagonal into two congruent triangles of area $\frac1{2k}=\frac1n$. This gives $2k=n$ triangles of equal area. ∎

chmmc-2019-power-02.title: Scale and add two triangles
chmmc-2019-power-02.body:
Take the unit square $[0,1]^2$ split into $n$ triangles of area $\frac1n$. Apply the vertical scaling $(x,y)\mapsto\left(x,\frac n{n+2}y\right)$. Areas scale by $\frac n{n+2}$, so each triangle now has area $\frac1n\cdot\frac n{n+2}=\frac1{n+2}$, and together they fill the rectangle $[0,1]\times\left[0,\frac n{n+2}\right]$.

The remaining part of the square is the rectangle of width $1$ and height $\frac2{n+2}$ (area $\frac{2}{n+2}$); a diagonal cuts it into two triangles of area $\frac1{n+2}$ each. We now have $n+2$ triangles of equal area $\frac1{n+2}$ splitting the square. ∎

chmmc-2019-power-03.title: Both cannot hold; one must
chmmc-2019-power-03.body:
*Not both.* If (2) held, infinitely many odd $n$ would be possible, so (1) would fail.

*At least one.* Suppose (1) is false. Then there is a smallest odd $n_0$ for which a square can be split into $n_0$ triangles of equal area. Applying the given fact repeatedly, every odd $n\ge n_0$ is possible. Hence the only odd $n$ that might be impossible are the finitely many odd numbers less than $n_0$, so (2) holds.

Thus exactly one of the statements is true. ∎

chmmc-2019-power-04.title: Angle sum
chmmc-2019-power-04.body:
The angles of the $n$-gon sum to $(n-2)\pi$. Each vertex of a convex polygon has interior angle less than $\pi$, so it cannot lie in the interior of a triangle or in the interior of a triangle's side: it is a corner of every triangle that contains it, and the angles of those triangles at the vertex add up exactly to the polygon's interior angle. Therefore the sum of all the angles of all $k$ triangles, which is $k\pi$, is at least the sum of the polygon's interior angles, $(n-2)\pi$. Hence $k\ge n-2$. ∎

(The same inequality holds for non-convex polygons; the squares in the next problem only need the convex case.)

chmmc-2019-power-05.title: Angle budget
chmmc-2019-power-05.body:
Suppose the unit square $ABCD$ is split into three triangles of area $\frac13$. Their angles total $3\pi$.

*Square corners.* Each corner of the square is a corner of some triangle, and the triangle angles there add up to $\frac\pi2$, so the four corners use $2\pi$.

*Other corner points.* Let $Q$ be a corner of a triangle that is not a corner of the square. If $Q$ is on a side of the square, the triangles around it fill a half-disc, so their angles at $Q$ total $\pi$ (a triangle with $Q$ inside one of its sides would fill the whole half-disc and $Q$ would be no corner). If $Q$ is interior, the triangles with a corner at $Q$ fill either the full disc ($2\pi$) or, if $Q$ lies inside a side of another triangle, a half-disc ($\pi$). So each extra corner point uses at least $\pi$ of the remaining $\pi$. Hence there is at most one extra point $Q$.

*Case 1: no extra point.* All triangles have their corners among $A,B,C,D$, so each has area $\frac12$ (or is degenerate), not $\frac13$.

*Case 2: $Q$ interior.* Then $Q$ must lie inside a side of a triangle $T'$ whose corners are square corners, so that side is a diagonal and $T'$ has area $\frac12$: contradiction.

*Case 3: $Q$ on a side, say $AB$ with $AQ=t$, $QB=1-t$.* Every triangle has corners among $A,B,C,D,Q$ and area $\frac13$. A triangle with only square corners has area $\frac12$, and $QCD$ has area $\frac12$, so the three triangles come from $QAC,QAD$ (area $\frac t2$) and $QBC,QBD$ (area $\frac{1-t}2$). Area $\frac13$ needs $t=\frac23$ or $1-t=\frac23$, not both. So all triangles come from one pair, say $\{QAC,QAD\}$, which overlap and are only two triangles: we cannot have three disjoint triangles.

All cases fail, so no such split exists. ∎

chmmc-2019-power-06.title: Write n in lowest terms
chmmc-2019-power-06.body:
Write $n=\frac{2^ma}{2^kb}$ with $a,b$ odd integers, $m,k\ge0$. Then $v_2(n)=m-k=-1$ means $k=m+1$, so $n=\frac{2^ma}{2^{m+1}b}=\frac{a}{2b}$.

So the set is $\left\{\frac a{2b}: a,b\text{ odd integers}\right\}$: the fractions which in lowest terms have denominator $\equiv2\pmod 4$. Conversely every such $\frac{a}{2b}$ has $v_2=0-1=-1$. ∎

chmmc-2019-power-07.title: Valuations of products and sums
chmmc-2019-power-07.body:
If $x$ or $y$ is $0$ the statements are immediate (using $M_2(0)=0$), so let both be nonzero and write $x=2^m\frac pq$, $y=2^k\frac rs$ with $p,q,r,s$ odd.

(a) $xy=2^{m+k}\frac{pr}{qs}$ with $pr,qs$ odd, so $v_2(xy)=m+k$ and $M_2(xy)=2^{-m-k}=M_2(x)M_2(y)$.

(b) $-x=2^m\frac{-p}{q}$ has the same valuation $m$, so $M_2(-x)=M_2(x)$.

(c) $M_2(x)\ne M_2(y)$ means $m\ne k$; say $m<k$. Then $x+y=2^m\left(\frac pq+2^{k-m}\frac rs\right)=2^m\,\frac{ps+2^{k-m}rq}{qs}$. The numerator is odd (odd plus an even number) and $qs$ is odd, so $v_2(x+y)=m=\min(m,k)$. Hence $M_2(x+y)=2^{-m}=\max\{2^{-m},2^{-k}\}=\max\{M_2(x),M_2(y)\}$. (If $y=0$ the claim reads $M_2(x)=\max\{M_2(x),0\}$, which is true.) ∎

chmmc-2019-power-08.title: Use multiplicativity
chmmc-2019-power-08.body:
From $xy=1$ we get $M_2(x)M_2(y)=M_2(1)=1$, so $M_2(y)=\frac1{M_2(x)}<1$ since $M_2(x)>1$.

Now $M_2(y)<1$ means $2^{-v_2(y)}<1$, i.e. $v_2(y)>0$. If $y$ is an integer (nonzero as $xy=1$), then $v_2(y)\ge1$ means $2\mid y$, so $y$ is even. ∎

chmmc-2019-power-09.title: Double counting dots
chmmc-2019-power-09.body:
Put a dot on each side of every rg-edge, close to the edge. Let $K_1$ be the number of dots inside the polygon.

*Count by edges.* A dot lies outside the polygon only next to a boundary rg-edge, so there are exactly $C_2$ dots outside. An interior rg-edge puts two dots inside and a boundary rg-edge puts one inside, so $K_1=2I+C_2$ with $I$ the number of interior rg-edges. Hence $K_1-C_2$ is even.

*Count by triangles.* Each inside dot lies in a triangle, and a triangle contains one dot for each of its rg-edges. By colour types: a complete triangle $rgb$ has exactly one rg-edge; triangles of type $rrg$ or $rgg$ have two; all other types ($rrr,ggg,bbb,rrb,ggb,rbb,gbb$) have none. So complete triangles contain exactly one dot and all other triangles contain $0$ or $2$ dots. Thus $K_1-C_1$ is even.

Therefore $C_1-C_2=(K_1-C_2)-(K_1-C_1)$ is even. ∎

chmmc-2019-power-10.title: Case analysis
chmmc-2019-power-10.body:
*At most one.* A point in $S_1$ has $M_2(x)<1$, while points of $S_2$ have $M_2(x)\ge1$: so $S_1\cap S_2=\emptyset$. A point in $S_1$ has $M_2(y)<1$, while points of $S_3$ have $M_2(y)\ge1$: so $S_1\cap S_3=\emptyset$. $S_2$ needs $M_2(x)\ge M_2(y)$ and $S_3$ needs $M_2(y)>M_2(x)$: so $S_2\cap S_3=\emptyset$.

*At least one.* Take any $(x,y)\notin S_1$; then $M_2(x)\ge1$ or $M_2(y)\ge1$, so $\max\{M_2(x),M_2(y)\}\ge1$. If $M_2(x)\ge M_2(y)$, then $M_2(x)\ge1$ and $(x,y)\in S_2$. Otherwise $M_2(y)>M_2(x)$ and $M_2(y)\ge1$, so $(x,y)\in S_3$. ∎

chmmc-2019-power-11.title: Use the max rule
chmmc-2019-power-11.body:
We use the *ultrametric inequality* $M_2(u+v)\le\max\{M_2(u),M_2(v)\}$ (equality when the magnitudes differ, by Problem 7c; when they are equal it follows from $v_2(u+v)\ge\min(v_2(u),v_2(v))$).

(a) $M_2(-x_1)=M_2(x_1)<1$ and $M_2(-y_1)=M_2(y_1)<1$, so $(-x_1,-y_1)\in S_1$.

(b) *Second point.* $M_2(x_2)\ge1>M_2(x_1)$, so $M_2(x_1+x_2)=M_2(x_2)\ge1$. Also $M_2(y_1)<1\le M_2(x_2)$ and $M_2(y_2)\le M_2(x_2)$, so $M_2(y_1+y_2)\le\max\{M_2(y_1),M_2(y_2)\}\le M_2(x_2)=M_2(x_1+x_2)$. Hence $(x_1+x_2,y_1+y_2)\in S_2$.

*Third point.* $M_2(y_3)\ge1>M_2(y_1)$, so $M_2(y_1+y_3)=M_2(y_3)\ge1$. Also $M_2(x_1)<1\le M_2(y_3)$ and $M_2(x_3)<M_2(y_3)$, so $M_2(x_1+x_3)\le\max\{M_2(x_1),M_2(x_3)\}<M_2(y_3)=M_2(y_1+y_3)$. Hence $(x_1+x_3,y_1+y_3)\in S_3$. ∎

chmmc-2019-power-12.title: Dominant term in the determinant
chmmc-2019-power-12.body:
Translate by $-A$ (translating by an element of $S_1$ keeps the classes): $B-A=(x_2,y_2)\in S_2$ and $C-A=(x_3,y_3)\in S_3$. The area is $\frac12|x_2y_3-x_3y_2|$.

From the definitions, $M_2(x_2)\ge M_2(y_2)$ and $M_2(y_3)>M_2(x_3)$, so
$$M_2(x_2y_3)=M_2(x_2)M_2(y_3)>M_2(y_2)M_2(x_3)=M_2(x_3y_2).$$
The magnitudes differ, so $M_2(x_2y_3-x_3y_2)=M_2(x_2)M_2(y_3)$. Hence
$$M_2(\text{Area})=M_2\!\left(\tfrac12\right)M_2(x_2)M_2(y_3)=2\,M_2(x_2)M_2(y_3)\ge2\cdot1\cdot1>1,$$
because $M_2(x_2)\ge1$ and $M_2(y_3)\ge1$. ∎

chmmc-2019-power-13.title: Colouring plus Sperner
chmmc-2019-power-13.body:
Suppose the square $ABCD$ is split into $n$ triangles each of area $\frac1n$. Colour each vertex of the triangulation red, green or blue when it lies in $S_1$, $S_2$, $S_3$ respectively.

*Boundary rg-edges.* On side $AB$ ($y=0$) every point has $M_2(y)=0<1$, so no point of $AB$ is in $S_3$; on $BC$ ($x=1$) $M_2(x)=1$, so points are in $S_2$ or $S_3$, not $S_1$; on $CD$ ($y=1$) $M_2(y)=1$ so there are no points of $S_1$; on $DA$ ($x=0$) $M_2(x)=0$ so points are in $S_1$ or $S_3$ (no $S_2$). An rg-edge needs one endpoint in $S_1$ and one in $S_2$, which is only possible on $AB$. Along $AB$ the colours go from $A\in S_1$ (red) to $B\in S_2$ (green) using only red and green, so the number of rg-edges on $AB$ is odd, and $C_2$ is odd.

*Complete triangle.* By Sperner's Lemma $C_1\equiv C_2\pmod 2$, so $C_1$ is odd; in particular there is a complete triangle, with vertices in $S_1,S_2,S_3$. By Problem 12 its area $K$ satisfies $M_2(K)>1$.

*Contradiction.* All triangles have area $K=\frac1n$, so $M_2(K)=M_2\!\left(\frac1n\right)=2^{v_2(n)}=1$ for odd $n$ (as $v_2\!\left(\frac1n\right)=0$), which is not $>1$. Contradiction, so no such split exists for odd $n$. ∎
